# Colony History
[italic]A short history of Barker's Lament for new arrivals, as the Herald's archive tells it.[/italic]
## The Name LV-376 was surveyed for the ore in its valley walls. The first prospecting crew reached the river in the 2150s, and their foreman, a man the records only call Barker, pitched camp in a dry arroyo because the ground there was flat. The first monsoon storm of the season sent a wall of water down the arroyo in the night. It took the camp, the core samples and two of his crew. The ore was still in the rock when the water went down, and the survivors gave the place the only name that seemed honest.
## Ore and Bread - [bold]Kelland Mine[/bold] opened on the richest of those seams and is still the biggest employer in the colony. Its bunks, office and lockup all sit at the pithead. - The colony was chartered under the United Americas to feed itself as well as dig. Hydroponics and the botany beds grow most of what the canteen serves. - The [bold]dam[/bold] holds back the river for water and power. Water treatment makes it safe to drink, and the micro atmospheric processing plant keeps the valley air fit to work in.
## Flag and Company - A military base sits at the edge of the colony behind a checkpoint. Which flag answers at the gate changes with the years, and residents learn to pass it without being asked twice. - Weyland-Yutani holds no charter here, but it keeps an office, a Weymart and a research site reached by tunnel the Company declines to describe. When the grid last ran short, the Company powered its own store first. Residents noticed.
## Hard Ground - In the monsoon, flash floods still come down the arroyos with little warning, and the river can climb the dam wall overnight. Nobody local camps in a dry bed. - Kelland works parolees alongside free miners under a Marshal Bureau programme, and the cells at the pithead are not for show. - It is an open secret that the scrapyard, and half the businesses around it, pay somebody for quiet. Nobody will say who on the record.
## The Press The Herald files from the journalist office and from wherever the story is. We keep the archive so that the next foreman who finds a nice flat spot in an arroyo knows why the place is called what it is.
